crossReferences.why: The same formulation, given as the reply when they demand to know when the promise will arrive.
Places the identical principle beside the statement that no town was destroyed without a known decree.
Applies the same rule to the individual soul rather than the community, with the same finality.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been treating as permanent because it has lasted a long time: a job, a neighbourhood, an arrangement in your family. Say to yourself, plainly, that it has an end date you do not know. Then do one small thing you would do if you knew it was closer than you think. One thing, today, not a plan.

studies.title: Messengers From Among You
studies.meaning: The condition attached to the messengers is easy to read past. They come from among you, which rules out the arrival of a being of another order and makes recognition possible and refusal harder. Their work is described with a verb meaning to follow a track. Then the response that secures the outcome is given as two things, not one: guarding oneself, and putting right. The second is active and outward. What follows is the Quran's recurring formula about fear and grief, in its conditional rather than its declarative form.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to the whole human line rather than to one audience, which is why it is phrased as a standing condition rather than an event. The Quraysh had objected that a messenger should be an angel or at least a man of greater means, and the wording answers that objection without arguing with it. No occasion of revelation is reported. The surah is about to give six such messengers in sequence, all of them local men.

keyTerms.note: From the root for following footprints. The messengers are described as tracking the signs rather than composing a message, which puts them in the position of guides reading ground already marked.
The root means to place a shield between yourself and harm. It describes protective care rather than dread, so the usual translation as fear catches only the reason for the action, not the action.
A verb for mending what is broken, used of reconciling parties and of restoring land to use. Paired with self-protection, it turns an inward posture into work done on something outside oneself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger in Arabia was a known figure with a defined role. Tribes sent men to carry terms, and the messenger's standing came from being one of the people he spoke for, since a stranger could not be trusted to deliver a message faithfully or to be held to account for it afterwards. To say the messengers would be from among you was to describe the only arrangement the audience already considered credible.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic here uses an emphatic conditional construction that combines two particles and adds a heavy verb ending, a form the Quran reserves for situations presented as certain to occur rather than merely possible. The English if or when cannot carry it. The grammar effectively says: when they do come, and they will.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is defined by ordinariness rather than by spectacle. A messenger is one of the people he addresses, which makes his life part of the message and removes the excuse that the standard was set by a different kind of creature. And the security promised is attached to a pair, guarding and mending, so an inward orientation is not accepted on its own. What settles the matter is whether anything was repaired.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same condition to jinn and humans together, messengers from among you relating My signs.
Records the objection this wording answers, that people refused to accept a human being as messenger.
Gives the same promise about fear and grief at the moment of the descent to earth.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing in your immediate reach that is broken and could be mended by you this week: a rift with a cousin, a promise you let lapse, a mess in a shared space that everyone steps around. Fix that one. The passage pairs inward care with outward repair, and only one of the two leaves evidence.

studies.title: Too Proud To Accept
studies.meaning: Two things are named and they are not the same. The first is calling the signs false, a judgement about content. The second is being too great for them, a posture that has nothing to do with evidence. The Arabic construction of the second verb implies turning away from something as beneath you. Placing them together suggests the classical reading that the verdict often follows the posture rather than producing it: a person decides they are above receiving instruction, and the arguments arrive afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The leading families of Quraysh objected repeatedly that the message had come to a man of no particular standing and that its early followers were poor men and slaves, an objection about rank rather than about content. This ayah sits directly after the promise made to those who guard themselves and put right, giving the alternative in the same breath. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, so it means to pronounce something a lie rather than merely to doubt it. The Quran uses it far more often than the word for disbelief, because it names an act of judgement made aloud.
The same root as the refusal earlier in this surah, in a form meaning to seek greatness for oneself. Followed by the preposition used here, it means turning away from a thing as unworthy.
The ordinary word for the people you keep company with and belong among. Applying it to the Fire describes belonging rather than sentence, which is a quieter and stranger idea than imprisonment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society was arranged by precedence, and precedence was performed daily. Who spoke first in the assembly, who was seated where at a feast, whose guarantee a stranger needed. A man of the leading clans could not be seen taking instruction from someone below him without the whole city noticing. The cost of accepting the message was therefore social before it was anything else, and it was paid in public.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs used here for denial and self-magnifying recur as a pair throughout the Quran, appearing together in this exact combination in several surahs. Classical commentators observe that the Book almost never presents rejection as a purely intellectual failure. Wherever the refusal is described at length, something about standing or pride is named alongside the argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is located partly in the will rather than entirely in the intellect. The passage does not say the deniers lacked evidence; it says they were too great for what they were given, which makes receptivity a moral condition. That is an uncomfortable claim, since it means a person can be perfectly capable of following an argument and still unable to accept it, and it explains why the Quran so often appeals to humility before it appeals to proof.

crossReferences.why: The first refusal in the surah, made on exactly these grounds and answered with expulsion.
Says God seals the heart of every arrogant tyrant who disputes the signs without warrant given.
Describes one who hears the signs recited, persists in arrogance as if unhearing, and mocks them.

studies.applyIt: Notice today whether there is anyone whose correction you would find it hard to accept, not because they are wrong but because of who they are. A younger colleague, a sibling, someone whose life you privately consider less successful than yours. Let one such correction land this week without adjusting for the source. That is the whole exercise.

studies.title: Where Are They Now
studies.meaning: A question is asked that expects no answer, pairing invention against God with denying His signs as the extreme of wrongdoing. Then a phrase commentators read in two ways: their share of the Book reaches them, meaning either what was decreed for them of lifespan and provision, or their portion as recorded. Both readings agree the point is that nothing is cut short. The scene that follows is the moment of death, and the envoys ask one question. The answer, when it comes, is a confession nobody demanded.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who maintained intermediaries at the sanctuary and expected them to intercede. Their objection to the message was not that God did not exist but that these figures had standing with Him. This ayah does not argue the point. It moves the question to the one moment when the arrangement will be tested, and lets the answer be given by the people who made it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for cutting leather to a pattern before stitching it. A fabrication in Arabic is something cut and assembled to fit, which describes invented religion more precisely than the word lie does.
From the root for paying a debt completely. Death is described as a collection of what is owed in its entirety, with nothing left outstanding, rather than as a seizure or an ending.
The verb for losing one's way, here with the objects doing the straying. What was relied on is described as having wandered off, which is a deliberately undignified word for a failed patron.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the security system of Arabia. A man without a strong protector had no recourse if he was robbed or killed, and the arrangement was renewed publicly so everyone knew who stood behind whom. Failing to appear when your client called was the worst thing a patron could do to his own name. The scene here uses that vocabulary exactly: the protectors are summoned at the one moment they are needed, and they are simply absent.
studies.didYouKnow: The testimony at the end is given by the people themselves, against themselves, and no accusation precedes it. This pattern recurs across the Quran's death and judgement scenes: witnesses are called, records are opened, limbs speak, but the decisive statement is often the person's own. Classical commentators note that the Book almost never needs to convict anyone who has not first agreed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the falseness of an arrangement not in an argument against it but in the moment it is required to work. Whatever a person leans on will either bear weight at that point or will not, and the Quran is content to let that be the test. It also insists that nothing owed is withheld in the meantime: the lifespan runs its course, the provision arrives, and the reckoning waits, which is a description of patience on God's part rather than of indifference.

crossReferences.why: The same scene of arriving alone, with the intercessors relied on described as cut away and lost.
Repeats the question directly, where are your partners now, and receives the same admission of absence.
Shows what was invented straying from them at the reckoning, using the identical verb for going astray.

studies.applyIt: Name, honestly, the thing you assume will hold you up if everything else fails. Savings, a qualification, a particular person, your own competence. Do not disparage it; most of these are real supports. Just ask whether you have quietly promoted it from a help to a guarantee. That distinction is the whole subject of this passage, and it is worth ten minutes.

studies.title: Each Curses Its Sister
studies.meaning: The instruction is to enter among communities that went before, jinn and human together, which places the newcomers in a lineage rather than in a category. Then the behaviour: each group entering curses the one before it. When all have arrived, the last address the first and ask for their punishment to be doubled, naming them as the cause. The reply grants the doubling and extends it to everyone, and closes with a clause that refuses to explain: but you do not know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a society organised entirely around following. A man's religion, trade, alliances and enemies came with his clan, and the defence that one had simply done what one's people did was the most natural thing a person could say. The surah has already recorded that defence in the mouths of those who appealed to their fathers. Here it is heard again, at the point where it is tested.

keyTerms.note: Communities are given a kinship word, since the noun for a community is grammatically feminine. Calling the earlier group a sister makes the cursing a family quarrel, which sharpens rather than softens the scene.

A verb for successive groups overtaking one another until all are gathered. It carries the sense of a crowd arriving in waves, each catching the one ahead, rather than of a single assembly convened at once.
The word means a fold or a doubling and can indicate more than twice over. The same root gives the Quran's word for multiplied reward, so the vocabulary of increase runs in both directions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society had no individuals in the modern sense. You were of a clan, and the clan answered for you: it paid your blood money, avenged your death, and bore your disgrace. Turning on your own people was close to unthinkable, and the poets treat it as the last collapse. A scene in which each generation curses the one that raised it would have struck the first listeners as a description of the end of the world.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply to the request for a double punishment does not deny it, adjust it, or defend the leaders. It grants the doubling and extends it to the petitioners themselves, then closes with a clause telling them they do not know. Classical commentators note that the Quran often answers a question in judgement scenes by widening it rather than by explaining it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Following is not accepted as a transfer of responsibility. Both parties carry a double weight, the one for leading and the one for choosing to be led, and the passage refuses to let the second be reduced to a misfortune. The mutual cursing makes a further point. What bound these groups together was never solidarity in the first place, since it dissolves the moment there is nothing left to gain from it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same complaint, we obeyed our chiefs and they misled us, with the same request for doubling.
Shows the leaders answering that they had no power over the followers, who chose to respond.
States that close friends will be enemies to each other on that Day, except those who guarded themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you do mainly because the people around you do it, and that you would not choose on your own. It does not have to be wrong. Just identify it accurately and say why you do it, without the usual softening. Owning a borrowed decision as yours is not the same as changing it, and it is the part that is actually available today.

studies.title: Humbly, And In Secret
studies.meaning: Two manners of calling are given rather than two times: lowered, and hidden from other people. A warning about transgressors follows, which the commentators attach to the manner of asking as much as to conduct in general, since the subject here is prayer. The second ayah adds a prohibition against wrecking what has been set right, then returns to prayer with two feelings held together, fear and longing. Mercy is then described as near, and the nearness is given a direction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah largely concerned with communities that were given a settled land and then ruined it. The prohibition against corrupting the earth after its ordering sits inside that argument, which gives it a historical edge a reader can easily miss. The commentators report no occasion for these two ayat and read them as instruction placed between the accounts of those communities.

keyTerms.note: From a root for lowness and for the udder of an animal, the part that yields when pressed. The word describes a bearing that gives way rather than a feeling, so it can be adopted before it is felt.

Concealment from other people rather than from God. Commentators read it as protecting the request from performance, since a prayer nobody hears cannot be made for anyone's benefit but the one praying.
A strong word, closer to greed than to hope, used of wanting something almost within reach. Paired with fear, it keeps the asking from collapsing into either despair or presumption.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public supplication in Arabia was a performance with an audience. Tribes called on their gods aloud at shrines and before battles, and poets composed the appeals. Rainmaking ceremonies were communal and noisy, and the noise was part of what was thought to work. Telling people to lower their voices and hide the asking removed the social function of prayer entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of fear and eager hope recurs across the Quran as a description of how the righteous pray, and in one passage it describes those who leave their beds at night to call on their Lord. The two words are almost never separated, and classical commentators treat the pair as a single instruction rather than as alternatives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is given a form as well as a content, and both parts of the form work against display. Lowering and hiding remove the two things that turn asking into performance, which is a precise diagnosis of how devotion goes wrong. The closing clause then locates mercy: it is not described as near in general but as near to those who do good, which ties the answer to conduct without making it a transaction.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pair of words for those who call on their Lord at night.
Shows Zachariah calling on his Lord in a hidden voice, the practice described here.
Earlier in the surah, calls for devotion offered sincerely to Him alone.

studies.applyIt: Ask for one thing tonight that you have never said out loud to anyone, in a voice only you can hear. Do not tidy the wording. The ayah asks for two things, lowness and privacy, and the second is easier than people expect once you notice how much of ordinary asking is shaped by an imagined listener.

studies.title: Call Him By His Names
studies.meaning: Two statements with an instruction between them. The names belong to God, they are described as the most beautiful, and the response asked for is to use them in calling on Him. The commentators note that the ayah neither lists them nor fixes their number. Then a second instruction, to leave alone those who distort the names, which is unusually restrained: no argument is prescribed, only withdrawal, with the outcome left where it belongs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators connect the ayah with the practice of deriving names for local deities from the divine name itself, which is what the word for distortion is taken to describe. The surah has spent much of its length on invented religion, and this ayah addresses the same problem at the level of vocabulary rather than at the level of ritual.

keyTerms.note: A superlative in the feminine, from a root for beauty and for what is good. It qualifies the names as a set, so the beauty is claimed for the whole vocabulary rather than for any single term in it.
The verb covers both calling someone by a name and calling on them for help. The ayah uses both senses at once, so naming and asking become a single action rather than two separate ones.
From a root for turning aside, related to the word for a grave niche cut off to one side. It describes bending a name away from its proper direction rather than denying it outright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names carried power in Arabia. A person's name announced lineage and often obligation, oaths were sworn by names, and poets attacked enemies by twisting theirs. Deities were addressed with strings of titles, and knowing the right form of address was thought to affect whether an appeal was heard. Instruction about which names to use was practical religious advice, not a matter of style.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran never gives a closed list of these names. The phrase occurs four times, always in the same form, and the familiar lists compiled later were drawn from across the whole text by scholars rather than presented anywhere as a single passage. The number most often cited comes from a report rather than from the Quran itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge of God is presented as vocabulary given for use, not as information to be held. The instruction is to call, which makes the names instruments of relationship rather than items of doctrine. And the handling of opponents is notably light: distortion is named as a real fault and then left alone, with no correction demanded, placing the matter between them and God rather than in a dispute to be won.

crossReferences.why: Runs a long sequence of the names, closing with the same phrase used here.
Says either name may be used in calling, since the beautiful names belong to Him.
States the same phrase as a single sentence about the one worthy of worship.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the divine names you rarely think about and use it once a day this week when you ask for something, choosing it to fit what you are actually asking for. The ayah joins naming to asking. Most people default to two or three names, and the difference a different one makes is worth noticing.

studies.title: Take What Comes Easily
studies.meaning: Three instructions arrive in one line, and the first is the most discussed. The word can mean pardon or what is surplus and easily given, so the commentators read it as accepting what people readily offer rather than pressing them, and also as forgiving. A warning about provocation follows, with a practical response: take refuge. Then a description of the God-conscious, who remember and then see, set against those who are dragged on without stopping.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the end of a long surah that has run through the destruction of earlier communities and the arguments of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) with his own people. These closing instructions are addressed to him about how to conduct that argument. The commentators record several reports about the first ayah, all of them turning on how a person deals with those who will not listen.

keyTerms.note: The root covers both forgiving and surplus. Commentators take it here as accepting what people offer without pressing them to their limit, which is why the same word can also mean pardon.
Not the uninformed. The word names people who act without restraint, and older poetry uses it for hot-headedness, so avoiding them means declining a fight rather than avoiding the uneducated.
A sudden jab, the word used of driving an animal forward with a point. It names the suggestion as brief and external rather than as a settled state, which is why the response given is immediate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab honour culture required an answer to every provocation, and skilled opponents provoked deliberately, knowing that an angry man could be manoeuvred into a costly quarrel. Poets baited each other in public for exactly that reason. Turning away read as weakness. The instruction to decline the exchange was not passive advice in that setting; it cut against the main mechanism of social standing.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to take refuge is followed two ayat later by an account of what taking refuge looks like from the inside: a person remembers, and then sees. The classical commentators follow that sequence closely, since the passage moves from an external command to an internal description of it working, which is unusual in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats provocation as something that happens to a person rather than as something they are. That distinction does a great deal of work: the sudden impulse is described as a jab from outside, and the response asked for is not suppression but relocation, taking shelter somewhere. And the contrast at the end is not between good people and bad, but between those who notice and those who are pulled along without ever stopping.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction with a reason, repelling harm with what is better.
Describes the servants of the Merciful answering the ignorant with peace.
Preserves a supplication for refuge from the promptings of devils.

studies.applyIt: The next time you feel the sharp pull to answer something, name it as a jab rather than as your own opinion, and wait until you have finished one slow breath. The passage puts a specific move in that gap. It does not say the provocation was unreal; it says the response is a place you go rather than a thing you win.

studies.title: Listen, And Be Silent
studies.meaning: A demand is reported and refused. When no sign is produced, the opponents suggest he should simply have devised one, and the reply concedes nothing about his own resources: he follows what is revealed, and does not compose. The text then names itself as insight, guidance and mercy. The second ayah turns to the listener with two instructions, hearing and silence, and attaches an outcome to them that is left as a hope rather than a promise.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah. The demand for a produced sign runs through the whole Meccan period. The commentators connect the second ayah with how people behaved during recitation, though the reports vary: some link it to the prayer, others to any occasion of hearing. What the two ayat share is a shift from arguing about the Quran to describing how it is to be received.

keyTerms.note: A verb for picking something out and gathering it for yourself. The taunt assumes composition, so the choice of word makes the accusation precise: they are asking him to produce, not to transmit.
The plural of a word for inner sight, formed like an instrument. It names the text as something you see by rather than something you look at, which is why the ayah pairs it with guidance.
A verb specifically for stopping your own speech in order to hear. It is added after the command to listen, so attention and silence are named separately and each is asked for on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was heard, not read, and audiences at the fairs listened with a critical ear and interrupted freely. Recitation was public and competitive, and a listener's noise was itself a form of judgement. Reports describe opponents at Mecca urging one another to drown out the recitation with talk and clamour. Telling listeners to fall silent addressed a real tactic, not merely a matter of manners.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the places in the Quran where the text describes the correct behaviour towards itself. The surah ends two ayat later with a prostration, one of the passages at which readers traditionally prostrate during recitation, so the instruction to listen is immediately followed by an instruction the body carries out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to produce a sign on demand defines prophecy negatively: the messenger's role excludes invention, and admitting that publicly costs him the argument in the short term. The passage then relocates the evidence into the text itself, calling it insight rather than proof. And the instruction to listen implies that something is transmitted in the hearing which cannot be obtained by discussing it afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Records the same demand to alter the Quran and the same refusal to change it.
Lists the specific signs demanded of him and the answer given to them.
Describes what happens to believers when the ayat are recited to them.

studies.applyIt: The next time you hear the Quran recited, whether you follow the words or not, stop what you are doing for the length of one passage and give it nothing but attention. No phone, no half-listening. The ayah asks for two separate things, hearing and silence, and most of us have got out of the habit of the second.
